📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rolling dice over Thanksgiving doesn't have to be dull, as these highly recommended board games prove. Want to avoid another family get-together battling over Bond Street in Monopoly? There are five beginner-friendly must-haves I'll always recommend for families, and these up the ante without overcomplicating things.

In a recent development, actually, these are often called 'gateway' games; they're ideal for newcomers and folks who don't have much experience beyond staples like Clue. Easy to learn but with enough nuance to keep you coming back for more, the five highly recommended board games I've listed below are a step up from old favorites yet don't feel overwhelming. They're not just for beginners, either. Some have reshaped the face of the industry with trend-setting mechanics, and I'd say they deserve a place amongst the very best board games.

Looking for something very straightforward? This is where I'd start. As noted in our Carcassonne review, the tile-laying game is "inoffensive family fun with heaps of replayability." Basically, you're building a patchwork kingdom and are trying to claim certain landmarks like cities or roads to earn points. Because you have a limited number of tokens to put on the board (and they stay there until those landmarks are finished), being flexible and knowing when to cut your losses is key.

If your family isn't up for anything complicated, this is my go-to recommendation. Herd Mentality is an easy-going and thoroughly silly board game about not standing out (which makes it great for those who hate the spotlight). You're all asked a simple question like "what is the best sauce?" and then have to scribble down an answer based on what you think everyone else will say. So long as you're in the majority, you get a point. That makes it a great warmup game or a decent choice if everyone's tired and sluggish after Thanksgiving dinner.

Industry observers note that this may be the ultimate party game for many, but it's also a great choice for family get-togethers; as we say in our five-star Codenames review, it's the "ultimate pick-up-and-play party game." After splitting off into teams, you've got to track down specific words laid out in a grid if you want to win - but the team-member guiding you can only provide a single clue that connects them. It's a lot of fun and real headscratcher for everyone involved.

Sources indicate that want something that's still easy-going but is more advanced? I'll always go to bat for this modern classic. Your aim's to complete train routes across North America for points, but there are limited tracks. That means you'll have to judge where your opponents want to go and cut them off at the pass, or risk having to go the long way around and waste precious time. Like I say in my Ticket to Ride review, it feels like a satisfying puzzle with a layer of strategy underneath it all.

It's not exaggerating to say that this is one of the most influential board games of the past 30 years, and it's had an immense impact on the hobby. This is a very clever strategy game about settling an uninhabited island with multiple ways to win, and while it's the most tactical option on this list, it's arguably the best - part of the reason we gave it such a glowing writeup in our Catan review is that you can keep coming back without having the same outcome.

I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

According to recent reports, slay the Spire 2, which released into early access earlier this year, is expanding once more with a major fresh beta update. This introduces the deckbuilder's first new character since launch - a whimsical musician armed with a bow - alongside two new modes, and more.

According to recent reports, when Slay the Spire 2 arrived back in March, it was to much enthusiastic acclaim. Eurogamer's Bertie Purchie is a major fan, and has trumpeted its successes on multiple occasions, calling the sequel's co-op mode "transformative". And it was a commercial hit too, managing to shift over 5m copies in just a month of release. All of which means there are plenty of eyes on Slay the Spire 2, eager to see what developer MegaCrit does next.

So far major updates have brought the likes of buffs, balance adjustments, art updates, UI improvements, bug fixes, and more - and MegaCrit has also made other substantial adjustments including the jettisoning of third act boss Doormaker, after it decided the encounter was overly complex. And now, as 2026 nears its conclusion, the studio has released its "biggest (beta) patch yet", including a sweep of major additions.

Industry observers note that as per MegaCrit's v0.113.0 patch notes, the headliner is The Fool; Slay the Spire 2's first new character, who's described as a "silly musician who wields a bow". Unsurprisingly, The Fool doesn't arrive in their final form, and the studio indicates it expects to make a "great number of content and balance changes" before the character is ready for the main branch.

Accompanying The Fool are two latest game modes: Blitz and Dread. Blitz is described as a "condensed and chaotic" mode focused on deckbuilding. Unlocked after completing an Ascension run of any difficulty, it comes with five levels of Ascension shared across all characters. "The Merchant's wares feel a bit off," MegaCrit teases, "the map is gone, and Gold no longer matters??".

According to recent reports, if you're looking for a more gruelling challenge, though, there's the "brutally difficult" newly introduced Dread mode, designed for players who've reached Ascension 10 on all characters, including The Fool. All ascension modifiers are enabled, according to MegaCrit, while bosses are stronger and buff all enemies found across their Act. And if that's still not enough to get your heart racing, MegaCrit notes curses will also pile up as you climb the Spire.

Beyond the headline stuff, v0.113.0 tweaks rest sites so they appear one floor earlier every act, and that's alongside the usual list of UI changes, art additions, nerfs, balance adjustments, and more. Full patch notes can be found on Steam.

According to recent reports, those players eager to put Slay the Spire 2's latest additions through their paces will need to enable the beta branch by right-clicking on Slay the Spire 2 in their Steam library and navigating to Properties > Game Versions & Betas and selecting 'public-beta' from the dropdown menu. MegaCrit notes the game's main branch has also been updated with all content and changes from the previous beta.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.

  • There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

Sources indicate that I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Industry observers note that spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

It has been revealed that you can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

Recent findings suggest that as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mainstay of the GTA series has been the presence of sex workers, but Rockstar Games has dropped this aspect for the newly released GTA 6.

As reported by Shack News, unlike most other games in the long-running franchise, you cannot hire a sex worker in GTA 6.

The outlet asked Rockstar about this decision, and received the following response:.

Sources indicate that "GTAVI is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run. While we have taken a lot forward from previous GTA titles, everything we have implemented in VI has been done to support the spirit of the story we wanted to tell, and the gameplay systems we wanted to expand upon - things like wanted system, the radio, robberies and car theft. Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTAVI, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasize as you play through Jason and Lucia's story.".

So, in other words, sex workers aren't included this time around because it wouldn't make sense for Jason or Lucia to pursue that, as they're already in a relationship — and that's a big part of the story.

As mentioned, they have been present in the series since 2001's GTA 3, and this will be the first 3D game to exclude them.

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is also the first game that centres on a couple, however, with the relationship between Jason and Lucia interwoven in the gameplay as well as being a key tenet of the narrative. It seems Rockstar didn't think sex workers would be conducive to this goal.

What are your thoughts on this? Tell us in the comments section below.

[source shacknews.com, via kotaku.com].

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of the launch of GTA 6, there was a whole lot of talk online about the Xbox "New Zealand trick" and how people could get early access to the game by switching their regions to New Zealand on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S.

We mentioned in various articles how it was a risky practice (against Xbox's ToCs), but one that had never traditionally resulted in any widespread bans, and it doesn't seem like either Xbox or Rockstar took any action at first glance.

As it turns out, a lot of people decided to give it a go for the latest Grand Theft Auto.

This is according to the folks at Ampere Analysis (via The Game Business), who report that over 2.1 million people played GTA 6 in the US and the UK before it was officially released.

As you can see from the graph above, it seems the vast majority of those were based in the United States, followed by the UK, Canada, Brazil and Mexico. Only around 100,000 people tried the trick on PS5 in the U.S. (where it's harder to implement and requires a separate account), whereas 1.5 million of them ended up using it on Xbox.

Ultimately, the existence of the New Zealand trick probably led to a bunch of increased sales for Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, but it also poses the question of whether Xbox might be forced to put a stop to it on Project Helix and beyond. As much it's a beloved feature, it's also being used in a way that wasn't originally intended.

Let's see what happens in the future, but for now, it's clearly made a lot of people happy this week!

Did you use the Newly introduced Zealand trick for GTA 6? Let us know your experiences with it in the comments.

According to recent reports, knowing how to get a jet in GTA 6 is essential information if you're planning to cause chaos, as taking control of one of these military aircraft is considered peak criminal behavior. While you'd expect that significant progress in GTA 6 would be required before you even had a chance of swiping such high-end hardware, you can actually go and help yourself to one pretty much as soon as you start the game. To try it yourself, here's how to steal a jet in GTA 6.

The location for a number of GTA 6 jets is the Mile Zero Air Station, which is found by heading west along the main road from the starting area, through Abismo Key, then on to Southwind and the military base itself.

Recent findings suggest that you can drive there in any vehicle, though I recommend not using your GTA 6 personal vehicle as it will get trashed and left inside the base, so steal a sturdy and reasonably fast vehicle for the job. Purchasing and equipping body armor from Ammu-nation will also improve your odds of surviving the initial stage.

Industry observers note that follow the route marked on my map above, which will lead you through some barriers on the road to a set of soldiers who will open fire, then take the first turning right and drive through more soldiers until you see a dirt pile ahead that you can hit to clear the security fences. This is also a Stunt Jump, though you don't need to complete it as long as you clear the perimeter and land on the runway.

According to recent reports, once on the runway inside the miliary base, drive straight ahead to where you'll see several GTA 6 jets parked up next to hangars. Pull up alongside one, jump out of your car and hop straight into the cockpit, before firing up the afterburner and turning onto the runway to take off.

Once you've taken control of your jet and got airborne, follow the prompt to retract the landing gear and you're away! Be aware that you'll have attracted at least a five-star GTA 6 Wanted Level with this theft, which could go up to six if you start blowing things up, so multiple military jets will be scrambled to shoot you down with homing missiles. I was barely able to reach the first bridge before getting blown out of the sky, but if you fly low and take evasive action you may fare better – good luck!

If you're looking for an impressive ride that's easier to obtain then here's how to steal the GTA 6 Paul Walker car, which you can then use to arrive in style at the various GTA 6 Strip Club locations around Leonida.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a newly introduced physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

In a recent development, for Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

Recent findings suggest that on release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

However, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

In a recent development, the answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Consumers were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

According to recent reports, in the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for customers. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

It has been revealed that "I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find newly introduced uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

In a recent development, when looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the problem of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got big as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

In a recent development, alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering owners.

"I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

With less than a week to go before GTA 6's hugely anticipated release, the game's final map - or at least a stylised poster version of it, depicting the state of Leonida's key landmarks - has surfaced online. It was reportedly snapped during Selfridge's sizable GTA 6's takeover, and is seemingly the physical map included in Rockstar's £350 collector's edition.

Fans have been pondering GTA 6's map for some time now, cross-referencing previous map leaks with official trailer footage in an attempt to gain some insight into the major landmarks and regions Rockstar has in store. And while the newly leaked map is far from granular, it does at least appear to confirm Leonida's rough layout and the key locations players can visit this time.

Assuming the map's veracity, it's all rendered in an art style somewhere between mid-century tourism poster and Adult Swim, featuring the phrase "The Goodtime State" up top - a riff on the actual Florida's nickname, The Sunshine State - while Leonida's most notable points of interest are interspersed with cartoon figures.

It has been revealed that there's a toking turtle (or possibly a tortoise - I'm no expert), a golfer proudly wearing assless chaps, a flying saucer, and more. I'll spare you the geographic details confirmed on the map in case you want to go in unspoiled. One point of amusement though: the way the map photo is cropped means fans searching for confirmation of an in-game Key West are still none the wiser.

It's not entirely clear where the wonkily angled photo originated from, but prominent Rockstar Games community insider Videotech, who shared the image on social media, suggested it came from a "naughty Selfridges employee" during Selfridges' GTA 6 takeover. The map itself appears to be the "double-Sided souvenir poster with map of Leonida" included in Rockstar's eyewateringly expensive GTA 6 Collector's Edition. This costs £350 and doesn't come with a copy of the game. Or assless chaps, for that matter.

In a recent development, this isn't the first time GTA 6's map - officially said to be twice the size of GTA 5's - has leaked online, although previous leaks have been notably more controversial. Earlier this year, a group calling itself CyberLeek shared unofficial gameplay and map details in the name of what it called "Gamers' Rights". In August, with Netflix's official GTA 6 unveiling looming, the group cashed out nearly £200,000 from its crypto scheme.

Amid all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion has been delayed until next week, meaning a verdict could arrive just as GTA 6 goes on sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that despite all the outrage and criticism around game developers and publishers using generative AI in gaming, a new report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC) calculates that as many as 40 percent of developers active in the industry use the controversial tools in their work.
  • That's according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from GDC, which gathers data from more than 2,300 respondents including, but not limited to, game industry professionals, made up of developers, producers, marketers, executives, and investors.
  • According to recent reports, the report notes that 57 percent of developers who say they do use it, use gen-AI for "text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that despite all the outrage and criticism around game developers and publishers using generative AI in gaming, a new report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC) calculates that as many as 40 percent of developers active in the industry use the controversial tools in their work. This is up four percent compared to the same report last year.

That's according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from GDC, which gathers data from more than 2,300 respondents including, but not limited to, game industry professionals, made up of developers, producers, marketers, executives, and investors.

According to recent reports, the report notes that 57 percent of developers who say they do use it, use gen-AI for "text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations". There appears to be a big split between triple-A studios that use gen-AI (with 27 percent of triple-A developers noting that they "feel encouraged or pressured" to use it) and indie devs, of which only nine percent say the same. Perhaps unsurprisingly - given how vocally against gen-AI a lot of 'frontline developers' have been - the tools are mostly used by "business operations and services, mobile-only studios, and free-to-play developers".

There seems to be a gap in the ages of those willing to use AI tools as well; per the report, over half (54 percent) of people 45 years or older reported using the tools - an eight-point increase from last year's survey. There is also more usage among men (45 percent) than women (33 percent).

In a recent development, what is perhaps more striking is that more people responded to the survey saying that they think AI is having a negative impact on games (55 percent) than responded saying they use the tech, suggesting a trend of caution rather than widespread adoption. Notably, respondents saying they are wary of the technology increased one percent since last year, so more people think AI is having a negative effect on the industry now than at the same time in 2025. Perhaps that's because of the sweeping layoffs we've seen across the games industry, often mentioned in the same breath as AI. Or the 'AI slop' that's been flooding Steam and pushing more traditional developers out. Orr some of the abysmal projects we've seen launch that have clearly used gen-AI assets.

"I did not get into a creative industry to hand over the creativity to an algorithm," mentioned one respondent from the UK when explaining why they don't use gen-AI tools. "I got into this industry to collaborate with creative people, not to have an advanced chatbot riff on the ideas of someone who was laid off," said another from California. "I believe that no one should have to read what no human has written and shouldn't have to see what no human has created," said yet another from Minnesota.

The use of generative AI remains controversial in the games industry, though with big companies like Epic and Microsoft doubling down on the tech, it seems this split between developers that want to embrace it and those that don't is only growing larger.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
  • The class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • The trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

The class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

The trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

"But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

In a recent development, you know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which right now looks likely to last until at least 2028.

Spoilers ahead for The Traitors: Latest Blood Finale.

According to recent reports, in just a few short years The Traitors has become one of my favorite shows on television. The Emmy-winning competition series just had its first season with non-celebrities called Newly introduced Blood, which aired on NBC (and streaming with a Peacock subscription). While fans have criticism for New Blood as a whole, I thought the two-episode finale was a thrilling conclusion. And I can't stop thinking about how the losers reacted to the news at the final Fire of Truth ceremony. Let's break it all down.

I'm counting the days for the next celebrity-filled Traitors cast to get on my TV, but Newly introduced Blood was a fun watch that really stuck the landing with its finale. At the Fire of Truth ceremony sweaty boy Victor and Traitor Katie were voted off, leaving just Wyatt, Abbey, and Shane in host Alan Cumming's castle. The latter was recruited via an ultimatum a few episodes ago, meaning he got to take home the full $246,300 prize pot.

Industry observers note that wyatt and Abbey were completely blindsided by this, and clearly had whiplash from thinking they won the money to realize they'd bee duped. They both cried in response, reminding me of Cirie's win back in Season 1. But after asking some follow up questions, and seeing Shane's tear-filled reaction to cheating his friends, the two Faithful sucked it up, walked over to him and hugged the season's winner.

Recent findings suggest that while it took until the reunion for Andie to forgive Cirie back in Season 1, I was so impressed by the way that Abbey and Wyatt were able to put their hurt feelings aside and give Shane the support he needed in this emotional moment. I truly can't stop thinking about the two of them walking over to him from opposite sides of the Round Table, and embracing him as he cried.

The high emotions for Newly introduced Blood make more sense than the celebrity seasons, as the prize pot is more a life-changing sum of money for civilians. So I would have understood if grudges were formed, especially by Abbey and Wyatt. As such, it's doubly impressive that wasn't the case, and they were able to support and forgive Shane.

It has been revealed that this sentiment of sportsmanship continued during the final moments of The Traitors: Upcoming Blood's finale, where all five of the finalists celebrated Shane's victory with champagne and fireworks outside the castle. While fruit gate was previously my favorite episode, I've got to say that this finale took the cake.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crimson Desert and DokeV developer Pearl Abyss is planning to further integrate generative AI into its workflow.

The South Korean studio said as much in its latest quarterly Earnings Letter, explaining that it had previously "validated game systems only after implementing them manually." Now, Pearl Abyss is using AI "to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," and argues the move "enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed.".

"However, AI serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity, while the core gameplay experience and actual content creation remain fully driven by our development team," the developer said.

When Crimson Desert first introduced, players spotted a crop of suspicious in-game images that looked like they were prompted into existence. Pearl Abyss soon explained that some "2D visual props" were generated with AI tools, but were always intended to be replaced with human-made art, before promptly patching them out of the hit open-world game.

Industry observers note that it seems Pearl Abyss is now even more keen on the controversial tech, however: "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality. AI is being utilized across various stages of development - including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization - and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline. We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously.".

Elsewhere in the letter, the studio stated its previously declared creature-collector DokeV is "targeting a launch in the second half of 2028" and we should hear more about it within the year. DokeV was initially targeting a 2023 launch a few years ago. Meanwhile, Crimson Desert is being prepped for a Nintendo Switch 2 launch "in the first half of next year.".

The use of generative AI in game development has been a hot topic for years, though it's only become more prevalent in recent months as 'AI slop' floods Steam and big companies like Epic Games proudly adopt the tech. A recent report even estimated that around 40 percent of active developers use AI tools in their work.

In a recent development, with GTA 6, Rockstar has created a game few other developers could even dream of competing with. That's partly down to the game's lengthy development cycle and massive budget, but you can also thank Rockstar's willingness to keep its veteran employees around when so many other studios are willing to lay off their most experienced developers.

21% of Rockstar, representing about 1,000 employees, have been at the company for more than 10 years, a spokesperson tells Bloomberg. Admittedly, that tenure only covers two major latest releases – Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 6 – but developers with a decade or more of experience at a single studio are becoming a rare breed.

Nintendo offers one of the most notable counter-examples, where the same five developers who worked on the original Super Mario Bros. were still in the credits of Super Mario Bros. Wonder nearly 40 years later. Rockstar hasn't been around for 40 years, but many of the names you'll find in the credits have been there since the PS2 era, when GTA fever had just started to reach its absurd highs.

Sources indicate that other publishers, meanwhile, are laying off even their most experienced staff by the bucketload. Devs like Fallout's Tim Cain are warning of the consequences of cutting off institutional knowledge even as Microsoft cuts off developers who'd been making megahits like The Elder Scrolls for decades. How can The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel live up to expectations when the people who know how to make Elder Scrolls games are constantly being laid off?

According to recent reports, clearly, Rockstar has been more willing to hang onto its veteran staff – unless, of course, we're talking about the 34 union-associated employees it fired in 2025. Disputes over those firings and the union itself are still ongoing, and ugly allegations about continued crunch at Rockstar are coming up as a result.

On top of all that, GTA 6 devs are "worried about getting laid off" even after "working on the biggest game of all time," and it's clear that there's no true insulation from the threat of layoffs when an executive decides your name is on the wrong side of a spreadsheet. Those fears remain even as GTA 6 itself stands as a monolithic example of what a group of experienced developers are truly capable of.

Grand Theft Auto 6 success isn't enough to stop the layoffs, former Square Enix exec argues, as Rockstar has "built the biggest, most expensive game of all time and now released it".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Legend of Zelda was in "dire straits" before Breath of the Wild gave the beloved series a massive second wind, according to two former Nintendo marketing leads.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next. Should Zelda lean into its carefully directed history - like the one brilliantly remade in Ocarina of Time - or keep the ball rolling with Breath of the Wild's wide open, spontaneous sandbox?

Nintendo of America's ex-director of social media marketing Kit Ellis and former public relations manager Krysta Yang chimed in on the discourse in their latest podcast (below), and explained that Zelda wasn't doing too hot before the Switch era.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately," Ellis stated in response to fans who reckon "the Zelda team ripped away" series staples, like classic dungeons and linear worlds, at the height of their popularity.

It has been revealed that "I remember, I was going to the focus groups where it was a really dark moment," Ellis continued. "The feedback was like, 'The fan base is dwindling. This is not bringing in new players.'".

Sources indicate that the Legend of Zelda was supposedly "shrinking," while "interest in the audience was getting smaller and smaller" with each new entry. "They had to do something dramatic," Ellis noted.

"This series was in dire straits. They were selling, like, nothing," Yang added.

The Zelda series was certainly never irrelevant, but there's a pretty big gap between the roughly 8m copies Twilight Princess sold at the beginning of the Wii generation, the roughly 3m copies Skyward Sword sold at the end of the console's life, and the 34m copies that Breath of the Wild sold just one console generation later.

It was a success so substantial it spawned a wildly ambitious sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, and even influenced the latest 2D Zelda, Echoes of Wisdom. Now that classic Zelda's back in the spotlight, though, I do hope Nintendo's able to slot the series' curated dungeons into whatever the next mainline game becomes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • It has been revealed that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

It has been revealed that as for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an glitch for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming update, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

UPDATE 17TH NOVEMBER: The Blood of Dawnwalker update 1.2 - the update that brings a New Game Plus mode, predominantly - is now available on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X.

Sources indicate that new Game Plus, as mentioned below, raises the level cap to 100, and scales enemies and regions in the game around you. Previously, the game was zone-scaled, so some zones were tougher than others. In New Game Plus, this will no longer be the case, so you can go and explore Xanthe's region at the back of Vale Sangora straight away, if you want to.

In a recent development, there'll be upcoming versions of equipment with new stats to find, and they'll be labelled with "NG+" so you know when you've picked one up. You can unlock New Game Plus from the main menu after choosing your base save and difficulty option. All of your accrued skill perks and abilities will be available to you at the start of the Withering Away quest in the game's prologue.

The full patch notes for Dawnwalker update 1.2 are:.

ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER: A Upcoming Game Plus mode is coming to vampiric RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker next week.

Developer Rebel Wolves has now detailed everything coming with The Blood of Dawnwalker's Enhancement 1.2, right now planned to go live sometime next week, and top of the list of changes is a New Game Plus for players who have already rolled credits on the game.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with Fresh Game+," the developer revealed earlier today. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over." Rebel Wolves is upping the level cap to 100 for New Game Plus, which will also have items with updated stats and enemies "balanced and scaled uniformly across all regions.".

Elsewhere in Update 1.2, the studio is making tweaks to "enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat," and improving terrain geometry to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration." The good (and hilarious) folks over at HDTVTest have been looking at the HDR Calibration settings for GTA 6 on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and they've discovered that the tool is actually slightly broken as things stand.

Some of the specifics go over my head a little bit to be honest, but in a nutshell, the figures that are displayed on the calibration tool don't fully translate into the game itself, leading to a potentially inoptimal picture.

As a result, they've published a new nine-minute video (which you can see up above) to explain the issues.

"The HDR calibration screen in GTA 6 can be misleading, because Rockstar's Max Brightness, Paper White and Black Levels settings interact in unexpected ways. To be clear, GTA VI's HDR rendering isn't broken… it's the calibration procedure that can give misleading results.".

The video goes step-by-step on how they analysed the challenges and tried to figure out the best possible HDR settings for GTA 6, and while their tests aren't fully concluded yet (there's another video to come in the future where they try multiple consumer displays), they've shared their initial best settings for displays capable of 1,000 nits or brighter.

Here are those three settings, but again, keep in mind that your TV must be capable of 1,000 nits of brightness or more, and that certain smart TV features or special HDR settings on your TV itself may interfere with the results.

According to recent reports, if your display isn't capable of 1,000 nits, do a bit of Googling to try and find out the specifics for your TV/monitor, and then times that figure by two in-game. So, if you're working with a maximum of 600 nits, set the figure as 1,200.

I have to be honest and say I'm not seeing a lot of difference here, but I've also got an old TV with a max brightness of just over 600 nits, not to mention I'm using a few image-altering features that may be playing havoc with the settings. It's also noted in the video that this is generally based on playing in the dark, rather than in a brightly-lit room.

Industry observers note that have a play for yourself and see what you think - there's clearly a lot of people who are very thankful for these settings on YouTube and beyond, so we wanted to at least make you aware of them. The reality is that you may need to still do a bit of tweaking to find the perfect sweet spot for your setup though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 has been censored to a fairly large extent in Japan, where the country's strict ratings system often sees nudity, sexual content, and graphic violence be toned down or removed entirely in video games.

To be clear, GTA 6 has been given Japan's highest 18+ age rating — but it's still had to make changes in order to ensure its release in the region.

For starters, Rockstar's latest is packed with full-on nudity — to a degree never before seen in a mainstream release — but in Japan, it's apparently impossible to remove the underwear of main characters Jason and Lucia, even when they're taking a shower.

The same is true of NPCs — everyone's always wearing at least one layer to cover up their privates.

Needless to say, the game's numerous sex scenes have also been censored. Again, it's a case of keeping clothes on — but some specific scenes have actually been cut completely.

Violence is next on the list. GTA 6 obviously features a lot of bloodshed but it's also rather gory, with accurate depictions of dismemberment and lethal physical trauma. It can all come across as particularly gruesome given how realistic the game looks.

In Japan, it seems as though most of this stuff is scaled back. There's less blood spray in general, and spilled blood doesn't stay in place very long.

It's a little unclear just how far this censorship of violence goes, but it's not uncommon for Japan to remove things like dismemberment — especially if a game's got a grounded setting.

It has been revealed that for what it's worth, GTA 6 does have several settings that let you change the amount of blood and gore that's on display. I assume that in Japan, these settings are applied at a censored standard by default.

Sources indicate that interestingly, though, drug use seemingly hasn't been touched. Japan's got very strict anti-drug laws, but illegal goods are still totally usable in GTA 6.

Sources indicate that did you see this censorship coming? Try not to go on a blood-soaked rampage in the comments section below.

Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • Sources indicate that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

Sources indicate that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

According to recent reports, thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock newly introduced rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make fresh, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

Netflix's long-gestating Magic: The Gathering animated series is called Planeswalker, and it's coming in 2027.

In a recent development, the title was revealed at MagicCon Atlanta, and Netflix shared a first look at the show on Twitter/X on 13th November. "Every great story begins with a spark. Here's your first look at Planeswalker, a new animated series based on Magic: The Gathering. Coming to Netflix in 2027", the company wrote, and shared a teaser, which you can see below:.

According to a synopsis shared with IGN, the series follows Chandra Nalaar, "a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past". It continues: "Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence".

In a recent development, netflix first announced a Magic: The Gathering series in June 2019, with Avengers: Endgame directors Joe and Anthony Russo attached, and it was originally due in late 2022. Two years in, the original showrunners departed over creative differences, and in September 2024, Netflix confirmed it had started again from scratch with Star Trek: Picard and 12 Monkeys showrunner Terry Matalas in charge.

In a recent development, IGN reports that Matalas, who most recently ran Marvel's VisionQuest, is running the show alongside Cindy Appel. Budapest-based studio DIGIC Pictures is handling the animation.

At the end of last month, we learned PUBG is also being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

Sources indicate that glover is a two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner, best known for Atlanta and Community. Krafton calls PUBG "one of the world’s most enduring gaming franchises", and says the game, which is credited with popularising the battle royale genre, holds seven Guinness World Records.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of Rockstar Games, has published GTA 6's day-one retail sales, and they're predictably astronomical and record-breaking.

Via BusinessWire, Rockstar and Take-Two announce that GTA 6's launch day sales, based on estimates through end of day on November 19, reached $3.79 billion, surpassing any other launch across all entertainment mediums and officially making GTA 6 the biggest entertainment launch of all time.

The companies also reveal that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies pre-release, which is another "newly introduced record across all platforms." For comparison, 2022 Game of the Year Elden Ring sold 30 million copies in three years.

Industry observers note that "It is with immense gratitude that we enter a newly introduced chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI," claims Rockstar co-founder and GTA veteran Sam Houser. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.".

Even though the industry has been anticipating GTA 6 to be the biggest game of all time, and very possibly the biggest entertainment product ever, for a while now based on the game's estimated budget of $1-1.5 billion, seeing these numbers become official is staggering.

Elden Ring was a massively successful game when it released back in 2022, and seeing its near-lifetime sales be eclipsed by GTA 6 in a single day is truly astounding no matter how inevitable Rockstar's success has always seemed.

As digital-only GTA 6 smashes records, GameStop CEO states move from physical copies "has hurt consumers" as they "should be able to sell" or trade purchases.

While GTA 6 has been receiving unbelievable praise and is technically considered one of the best video games of all time according to Metacritic, that certainly doesn't mean it's immune to criticism.

Recent findings suggest that one of the significant talking points both before and after launch has been that it's a 30FPS experience across all Xbox and PlayStation consoles, and if you're going from 60FPS back to 30FPS, there's definitely an adjustment period. Some people are absolutely fine with that, while others are finding it extremely difficult to go back.

For what it's worth, our friends at Digital Foundry have been analysing this in depth today:.

Rockstar Games has already confirmed recently that even the PS5 Pro doesn't come close to running GTA 6 at 60FPS due to the system's processor not being powerful enough, so we might be forced to wait until the next generation of consoles (and PC) before the game will become playable at 60 frames per-second.

Recent findings suggest that "The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game’s visual fidelity. While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates.”.

Recent findings suggest that with all of this in mind, we're interested to hear what you think about playing games at 30FPS on Xbox, PlayStation or anywhere else. It's becoming much more common that 60FPS is the default these days, but there are still some phenomenal 30FPS-only experiences out there, and it's a shame to think people are missing out on them.

I personally much prefer playing at 60FPS if I can, and there are certain games I will avoid at 30FPS until they get a patch down the line (like Mafia: Definitive Edition), but when it comes to industry-defining masterpieces like Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto VI, the last thing I'd want is for them to scale back the detail in order to squeeze in a 60FPS mode.

Recent findings suggest that so, what do you think? Tell us in the poll above and in the comments section below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Call of Duty Endowment is marking Remembrance Day and its 17th anniversary by encouraging Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone players to pick up its Valor Pack, with all of Activision's net proceeds going towards helping veterans find jobs.

The Call of Duty Endowment Valor Pack - which has been available since Modern Warfare 4 launched on 23rd October - was designed by the Endowment and Infinity Ward with US Marine Corps veteran and Medal of Honor recipient Kyle Carpenter in mind.

The items include a melee weapon blueprint inscribed with "Worth Fighting For", plus items called Relentless and Still Standing.

According to the Call of Duty blog, 100 percent of Activision's net proceeds from the pack (after VAT and sales tax) go to the Endowment.

To mark Remembrance Day, players who owned it and launched either game before 6pm GMT on 12th November also received double XP tokens and a DMZ survival kit.

"Veterans bring incredible skills into the workplace after military service," remarked Carpenter.

The Endowment, which supports veterans in the UK as well as the US, says it has now helped place more than 180,000 into "high-quality jobs", and wants to reach 200,000 by 2030.

According to recent reports, other partners are also raising money, with Pilot's round-up campaign raising more than £4.7 million ($6 million) for the Endowment since 2019. Polaris will also donate around £19,500 ($25,000) if players collectively complete 5 million rides in its DAGOR vehicle across Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone by 25th November.

It comes two weeks after Activision apologised to bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it would remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Players discovered that the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died.

Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet recently declared it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

Sources indicate that unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that plan release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the company has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental problems.

Industry observers note that unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

The grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is right now harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people.".

Recent findings suggest that the manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture.".

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the firm code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games.".

Industry observers note that it's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

Industry observers note that according to Insider Gaming, the project is in early development at Ubisoft Montreal under the codename Spades. It’s one of three new projects reportedly in production at the studio, and sources suggest a second of those is also set in the Rainbow Six universe. Eurogamer hasn’t been able to verify the report.

It’s not yet clear what form the new game will take, but Insider Gaming’s sources noted it's "likely Vegas 3 rather than a remake" of an existing game. Insider Gaming expects it will be several years before Ubisoft officially announces a new Vegas game.

Rainbow Six Vegas launched in 2006, followed by Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008. Since then, the series has centred on 2015's Rainbow Six Siege, and in August, Ubisoft declared Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player, turn-based spin-off from Ubisoft Paris due in 2027.

Rainbow Six now sits under Vantage Studios, the Ubisoft subsidiary set up last year that also oversees Assassin’s Creed and Far Cry, and in which Tencent holds a 26.32 percent stake.

According to recent reports, last week, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on two upcoming Assassin's Creed games: one set in ancient Rome, and a mobile spin-off set in Jerusalem. The leak came less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are at the moment no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

Police in Shanghai, China have reportedly arrested 13 people in connection with an alleged criminal scheme selling counterfeit Final Fantasy 7 figures.

It has been revealed that first reported by local Shanghai-based publication Shangguan News (translation via Automaton), in May Shanghai police began receiving complaints about Final Fantasy 7 Tifa Lockhart figures purchased from an online store that didn't match-up with the official toys licensed by rights holder Square Enix. Police reportedly verified with Square Enix that the seller had not been authorized to sell the figures, which appear to be nearly identical to an official Square Enix product, although seemingly without the articulation points that allow you to change the position of arms and legs. Here's a comparison via Dexerto's Twitter account:.

Police have arrested 13 people accused of selling counterfeit Final Fantasy 7 Tifa Lockhart figures The Chinese sellers reportedly charged higher prices by including extra faces, hands, and accessories not found with the official figures https://t.co/AE1IyS0wi9November 19, 2026.

Shanghai police have reportedly busted more than 30 similar cases of counterfeit figures or figurines in 2026 alone, resulting in more than 140 arrests and 70 million yuan, or $10.5 million, in seized assets.
